summary:
Selene Vantage is an interactive lunar site-analysis tool for rapidly comparing candidate landing locations based on time-dependent Sun and Earth Visibility. It uses NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides to calculate the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth from selected lunar coordinates, then identifies visibility windows, durations, and periods when both are above the lunar horizon. Users may compare two locations across periods ranging from hours to approximately one lunar day, explore curated Apollo and CLPS locations, or enter custom coordinates themselves.

The project addresses the challenge by providing a reproducible, accessible first-pass method for evaluating how lunar location and timing affect illumination and Earth visibility. This is important because sustained sunlight and line-of-sight to Earth are key considerations when assessing potential landing and operational sites. Selene Vantage is intentionally a screening tool rather than a full engineering feasibility model; terrain, hardware orientation, power generation, and communications link budgets are outside its current scope due to the events time limit.
details:
Selene Vantage is an interactive, browser-based lunar site-analysis tool designed to compare the time-dependent geometric visibility of the Sun and Earth from different locations on the Moon.

Users can select two locations from a catalogue of 13 documented Apollo and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) locations, they may also enter their own custom coordinates. They can specify an observation date, start time, duration as well as different sampling intervals. The application then queries NASA/JPL Horizons for the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth as observed from the lunar surface.

The calculated elevations are compared against a 0-degree geometric horizon. Selene Vantage identifies visibility windows, estimates rise and set times, calculates total and percentage visibility durations, measures the longest continuous visibility periods and gaps, and identifies periods when both the Sun and Earth are simultaneously seen. Results are presented through interactive Plotly graphs, comparison metrics and as downloadable CSV data.

The project provides an accessible first-pass screening method for examining how lunar location and timing affect solar illumination opportunities and direct Earth line of sight. Its intended impact is to help users explore and compare candidate locations before undertaking more detailed mission-specific engineering analysis.

The application was developed using Python 3.13.9, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas and Requests, with Git/GitHub for version control and automated testing using pytest.

Its creative element is the integration of live planetary ephemerides, a documented historical and planned lunar-site catalogue, custom coordinates and time-dependent comparison metrics into one accessible application. Particular care was taken with coordinate conventions, source traceability, UTC time handling and distinguishing actual landing positions from planned destination-regions reference points.

The current model evaluates geometric visibility only. It does not incorporate local lunar terrain or LOLA elevation models, terrain shadows, solar-panel orientation, electrical power generation or communications link budgets. These are identified as areas for future development.
